docs.creator: Heyerdahl, Thor
description: Kon-Tiki is the record of an astonishing adventure -- a journey of 4,300 nautical miles across the Pacific Ocean by raft. Intrigued by Polynesian folklore, biologist Thor Heyerdahl suspected that the South Sea Islands had been settled by an ancient race from thousands of miles to the east, led by a mythical hero, Kon-Tiki. He decided to prove his theory by duplicating the legendary voyage. On April 28, 1947, Heyerdahl and five other adventurers sailed from Peru on a balsa log raft. After three months on the open sea, encountering raging storms, whales, and sharks, they sighted land -- the Polynesian island of Puka Puka. Translated into sixty-five languages, Kon-Tiki is a classic, inspiring tale of daring and courage -- a magnificent saga of men against the sea. Washington Square Press' Enriched Classics present the great works of world literature enhanced for the contemporary reader. This edition of Kon-Tiki has been prepared by an editorial committee headed by Harry Shefter, professor of English at New York University. It includes a foreword by the author, a selection of critical excerpts, notes, an index, and a unique visual essay of the voyage

docs.description: When Thor Heyerdahl landed his Kon-Tiki  raft on a tiny South Pacific atoll in 1947, he had wrought the missing link in the massive chain of evidence he was forging in support of his theory on the origins of the Polynesian people. "American Indians in the Pacific" is his definitive and controversial work on these cultural origins of the Polynesian people.      He presented numerous early photographs and depictions,  cultural and racial similarities,  even botanical parities, all correlating North/South America with Polynesia, mainly the Marquesas  and Easter Islands. His contention being that Polynesian people were a mixed population descending from two groups of immigrant people who came to Polynesia from the Americas. One group, from the Pacific coast of South America and a second group from coastal Pacific Northwest of North America.    Despite the overwhelming evidence he conferred, his theory was never really accepted by main-stream science. Sometimes even hostilely criticized.    However, Heyerdahl always held irrefutable evidence that could never be addressed by his critics. As he stated; he could possibly understand that if a sweet potato could conceivably float from it's original homeland of Peru, carried by the Humbolt Current to the far reaches of the eastern Pacific, it could become a universal Polynesian food staple. But sweet potatoes die in salt water. So how did it migrate unaided? But that aspect aside, if the sweet potato somehow accomplished this impossible unaided migration to the far east reaches of Polynesia, how was it possible that it's name is universally the same as it's original Peruvian term - Kumara?  Heyerdahl asks; how did that name float with the tuber, alone across the vast Pacific?    This is a long book but it will be enjoyed by anyone who is interested in ancient human history, who prefers to be led by evidence rather than academic dogma.
docs.title: American Indians In The Pacific, The Theory Behind the Kon-Tiki Expedition

"'Am going to cross Pacific on wooden raft to support a theory that the South Sea islands were peopled from Peru. Will you come?...Reply at once.' That is how six courageous and inquisitive adventurers came to seek a dangerous path in order to test a hypothetical theory. On a primitive raft made of forty-foot balsa logs, named 'Kon-Tiki' in honor of a legendary sun king, Thor Heyerdahl and his five comrades set out, risking their lives to prove that ancient Peruvians could have made the 4,300-mile voyage to the Polynesian islands on a raft similar to theirs. Every page of Kon-Tiki--from the building of the raft and the dangerous adventures at sea, to a spectacular crash landing and the dances of the native islanders--chronicles of a true-life, spellbinding escape from the twenty-first century"--Cover, p. 4

docs.description: For over 65 years, the United States war machine has been on auto pilot. Since World War II, the world has believed that US foreign policy means well, and that America’s motives in spreading democracy are honorable, even noble. In this startling and provocative book from William Blum, one of the United States’ leading non-mainstream chroniclers of American foreign policy and author of the popular online newsletter, The Anti-Empire Report, demonstrates that nothing could be further from the truth. Moreover, unless this fallacy is unlearned, and until people understand fully the worldwide suffering American policy has caused, we will never be able to stop the monster.
